hints: Focus on the clue that methylamine has similar chemical properties to ammonia, so its salt should behave like ammonium chloride.
Recall what happens when ammonium chloride, $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$, is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide to release the free base.
Swap ammonia for methylamine in that familiar reaction, then match the remaining ions to form a sodium salt plus water.
walkthrough:
**Recall the familiar ammonia test**

Think of this as the classic test for an ammonium salt. A stronger base displaces a weaker base from its salt.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Apply the same idea to methylamine**

Methylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, is also a base, just like $\text{NH}_3$. Its salt contains the $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$ ion, which will donate a proton to $\text{OH}^-$.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Put all the products together**

The free base $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ is released. The spectator ions $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ join to make $\text{NaCl}$, and water forms too.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

options.A: Incorrect. This is the product set for ammonium chloride, not methylammonium chloride. You get ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, only if you start from $\text{NH}_4^+$. Here the cation contains a methyl group, so the base released must be methylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$.
options.B: Incorrect. There is no source of carbon for hydrogencarbonate, $\text{HCO}_3^-$, in this mixture. This option also wrongly gives ammonia instead of methylamine. It mixes up carbonate chemistry with amine salt chemistry.
options.C: Incorrect. Hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$, is a strong acid and cannot exist alongside a strong alkali like $\text{NaOH}$. They would neutralise immediately to give $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. This option is like trying to reverse the salt formation while ignoring the NaOH.
options.D: Correct. By analogy to $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH}$, the hydroxide removes a proton from $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$ to regenerate free methylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, leaving $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Well done for spotting the direct analogy.
